The Torah is a 3-sentence aphorism (Likutay Moharan Vol. 1, Torah 223) about the two levels of tzaddik — one who petitions and one who decrees — and equates the decree-mode with the Priestly Blessing formula.

additions.reason: This is the dominant concept of Torah 223. The Rebbe distinguishes a higher level of tzaddik who does not merely request from God but can decree — saying 'I say it shall be so.' This is the concept to which the bechina of the Priestly Blessing formula is applied. The node represents the capacity of holy decreeing speech in the tzaddik.
additions.source_quote: יֵשׁ צַדִּיק שֶׁיָּכוֹל לִגְזֹר וְלוֹמַר: אֲנִי אוֹמֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן

additions.reason: The Priestly Blessing formula — specifically the phrase 'אָמוֹר לָהֶם' (say to them) — is the explicit bechina target in the Torah text. The Rebbe interprets this as: the Kohen does not petition God to bless Israel but actively declares the blessing as established fact ('I say it shall be so'). This is the same essential nature as the tzaddik who decrees: both are authoritative, performative holy speech. The bechina is explicitly marked with 'וְזֶה בְּחִינַת.'
additions.source_quote: וְזֶה בְּחִינַת (במדבר ו׳:כ״ג): כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ וְכוּ' אָמוֹר לָהֶם – הַיְנוּ שֶׁאֲנִי אוֹמֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן

additional_observations: The Torah text mentions a contrasting concept — the ordinary tzaddik whose petition (בַּקָּשָׁה) may or may not be heard — but this is framed as the narrative contrast/foil, not as a bechina node. The Rebbe cites the Zohar ('זִמְנִין דְּשָׁמַע וְזִמְנִין דְּלָא') to establish why ordinary petition can fail, before introducing the higher mode. This contrasting concept (בַּקָּשָׁה / petition) is an eitza-type contrast (what leads to failure vs. what succeeds), not a bechina parallel — so it is correctly excluded from the bechina package.

The Torah has no evil/sitra achra component. There is no evil mirror package — the negative pole is simply the limitation of ordinary petition, not an active evil force. The polarity structure here is good vs. a lesser-good, not good vs. evil.
